headline: Dono is tono with the t voiced to d by rendaku.
Mugen may be a learned borrowing from Chinese 無限 (wúxiàn, literally “without + limit”), first cited to 1881 as a translation of English infinite.
Tenrankai is 展覧 (tenran, “exhibition”) plus 会 (-kai, “gathering”).
Tera appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE; some sources derive it from an ancestor of Middle Korean 졀 (jeol), likely Baekje.
Kago appears to be an uncertain element ka plus 籠 (ko), with ko voiced to go.
Ureshii might come from 熟れる (ureru, “to ripen, mature”) plus しい, though it is unclear how “feeling mature” matches “glad”.
Sukizuki is a reduplication of 好き (suki, “fondness”).
Chūsei is 中 (chū) plus 性 (-sei).
In yōgan, 溶 is a daiyōji replacing 熔.
Hiruma is 昼 (hiru, “daytime; noon”) plus 間 (ma, “space; period”).
Tsui, “pair”, is from Middle Chinese 對 (MC twojH).
Shiro's derivation is unknown; the reading first appears in 794 CE when 山背 (Yamashiro) was renamed 山城 by Emperor Kanmu.
Hikikaesu is 引く (hiku, “to pull”) plus 返す (kaesu, “to return; to repeat”).
Boro is described as shortened from ぼろぼろ (boroboro), first attested in 1736, though a homophone for beggar monks, 梵論, dates from the early 1300s.
Tsuya is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tuya.
Koi went from kopi through kofi and kowi to koi, from the stem of 恋う (kou, “to love, yearn”).
Tōrikakaru is 通る (tōru, “to pass through”) plus 掛かる (kakaru).
Utsuru, “to be photographed”, is a doublet of 移る (utsuru, “to move; to transfer”).
Shinkei was first used in the Kaitai Shinsho of 1774 by Sugita Genpaku and others, translating the Dutch zenuw.
Tatakai is the continuative stem of 戦う (tatakau, “to fight”).
Makeru is from Old Japanese 負く (maku), from Proto-Japonic *mak-a-.
Nagabiku is 長い (nagai) plus 引く (hiku).
Bō, “pole”, is from Middle Chinese 棒, the goon pronunciation, so likely an earlier borrowing.
Gurasu is English glass, a doublet of ガラス (garasu), from Dutch.
Katsuryoku is 活 (katsu, “life”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).
Shukushō is 縮 (shuku, “shrink,” “reduce,” “shorten”) plus 小 (shō, “small,” “little”).
Joshi is 助 (jo, “helper”) plus 詞 (shi, “word”).
Inki is borrowed from Dutch inkt, ultimately from Ancient Greek énkauston, “burned-in”.
Gutai is Middle Chinese 具體, literally “arrange + body”, repurposed in 1881 as a translation of English concrete.
Tsuru, “to fish”, is cognate with 吊る (tsuru, “to hang”).
Tondemonai is considered a shift from 途でもない (to de mo nai, literally “that is not even the way”).
